document.title: Comments of Olabanji John Ogunyemi in response to the 06/18/2026 Show Cause Order

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
BEFORE THE
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
)
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.
)
Docket No. EL26-67-000
)
COMMENTS OF OLABANJI JOHN OGUNYEMI
Olabanji John Ogunyemi submits these comments in the above-captioned proceeding. On 
June 18, 2026, the Commission directed PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) and the PJM 
Transmission Owners to show cause why PJM's Open Access Transmission Tariff remains just and 
reasonable without provisions addressing (a) the application process, study procedures and 
operational requirements for transmission service on behalf of large loads; (b) transparency of 
Network Upgrade costs and a pro forma cost recovery agreement; (c) transmission services for 
flexible large loads; and (d) the rates, terms and conditions of service applicable to interconnection 
customers serving electrically proximate large load or co-located load.  PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211, at P 3 (2026) (Show Cause Order). The Commission also directed PJM 
to report on how it intends to ensure that adequate generation will be available to serve existing and 
new large loads. Id. P 4.
These comments address one question that runs through each of those issues: whether the 
generation built to serve large loads can be financed. My comments are offered from the 
perspective of the lenders, tax equity investors and tax credit buyers whose capital that generation 
depends on.
I.
INTEREST OF THE COMMENTER
I am a project finance professional working on solar and battery storage projects in the 
United States. My work includes sizing construction and term debt for solar projects, preparing the 
documentation lenders and tax credit buyers require before they commit capital, and managing 
operating solar assets and the reporting their lenders rely on. My experience is with distribution-
1

connected projects in the Midwest and New England, outside the PJM region, but the financing 
tests these projects must pass are the same nationwide. I submit these comments in my personal 
capacity. They do not represent the views of any employer, client or counterparty, and I am not a 
party to this proceeding.
II.
SUMMARY
Much of the new generation that will serve large loads, including data centers, will be solar 
and battery storage, because those resources can be built fastest. The U.S. Energy Information 
Administration reports that developers planned to add 43.4 GW of utility-scale solar and 24 GW of 
battery storage in 2026, out of 86 GW of planned additions.[1] Whether that generation is built 
depends in large part on whether it can be financed. Capital providers commit only against terms 
they can underwrite: a known path to interconnection and service, a cost exposure they can 
quantify, and a schedule that fits the project's other deadlines. I support reforms that give large 
loads, and the generation serving them, those three things, and I urge the Commission to direct PJM 
to set them out in its Tariff.
III.
COMMENTS
A.
Study procedures should have defined timelines, because federal law now fixes a 
completion deadline for solar (Show Cause Order P 3(a)).
Public Law 119-21 ends the clean electricity investment and production credits for wind 
and solar facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, where construction begins after July 
4, 2026.[2] For a solar project financed against the credit, a delay in interconnection or service 
studies is no longer only a delay. It can cost the project its credit, and with it a large part of the 
capital that makes the project financeable. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory reports that the 
median project built in 2025 took 61 months from interconnection request to commercial 
operation, and that only about 13 percent of the capacity that requested interconnection from 2000 
to 2020 had reached commercial operation by the end of 2025.[3] The Commission has already 
accepted, in Southwest Power Pool's tariff, a process it found "reasonably provides a flexible, 
2

expedited,  and  separate  serial  interconnection  process  that  will  facilitate  the  prompt 
interconnection of generating facilities that are limited to serving" a high impact large load.[4] I 
encourage the Commission to require that the procedures PJM adopts for large loads, and for the 
generation serving them, include defined study timelines of that kind, so that projects can plan 
against the statutory deadline with confidence.
B.
Cost transparency should extend to estimates that capital providers can rely on 
(Show Cause Order P 3(b)).
I support the Commission's focus on transparency of Network Upgrade costs and on a pro 
forma cost recovery agreement to mitigate cost shifting. I would add that, for financing purposes, 
the value of transparency depends on whether cost estimates are firm enough to be relied on. Debt 
is sized against a project's expected costs and cash flows; an upgrade estimate that can change 
materially after financial close is a risk lenders price conservatively or refuse to take. Research on 
interconnection costs has found that projects that withdrew from the queue faced substantially 
higher estimated interconnection costs than those that completed the study process.[5] A pro forma 
agreement with estimates that are binding, or bounded within a stated range, would let capital 
providers size their commitments with confidence while still protecting other customers from cost 
shifts.
C.
Clear services for flexible large loads would support storage financed alongside 
them (Show Cause Order P 3(c)).
Battery storage is particularly relevant to transmission services for flexible large loads. 
Under Public Law 119-21, the termination that applies to wind and solar does not apply to energy 
storage technology,[6] so storage will remain financeable against the federal credit after 2027. 
Storage paired with a large load can let that load limit its use of the transmission system under the 
conditions the Commission describes. Clear rules defining how such a flexible load is served, and 
how its storage is treated, would let that storage be financed on firmer ground and built where it can 
do the most for reliability.
3

D.
Terms for generation serving electrically proximate or co-located load should be set 
out in the Tariff (Show Cause Order P 3(d)).
From a financing perspective, the most important feature of the rates, terms and conditions 
for interconnection customers serving electrically proximate or co-located load is that they are 
defined in advance. A construction lender sizes its loan, sets its draw conditions and fixes its 
conversion tests against the project's expected interconnection and service arrangements. Where 
those arrangements depend on negotiations whose outcome cannot be known at financial close, the 
lender either discounts the project's value, requires additional equity or reserves, or declines to 
lend. Defined Tariff terms would allow generation serving these loads to be underwritten on the 
same basis as other generation, and would reduce the number of projects that stall before financial 
close.
E.
PJM's assessment of adequate generation should reflect delivered output (Show 
Cause Order P 4).
In reporting how it will ensure adequate generation to serve large loads, PJM should 
account for the output that generation actually delivers, not only its nameplate capacity. Operating 
solar plants do not always deliver their expected output. A National Renewable Energy Laboratory 
study of 8.5 GW of U.S. photovoltaic systems found median availability of 0.99 but tenth-
percentile availability of 0.95, meaning a tenth of systems lost at least five percent of production to 
unavailability alone.[7] Accounting for delivered output would give a more accurate picture of the 
generation available to large loads, and would reward owners who keep their plants performing.
IV.
CONCLUSION
New solar and storage generation can help meet the demand of large loads quickly, but only 
if it can be financed. I respectfully urge the Commission to direct PJM to adopt Tariff provisions 
that give large loads and the generation serving them (i) study procedures with defined timelines, 
(ii) cost estimates that capital providers can rely on, (iii) clear services for flexible large loads 
paired with storage, and (iv) defined rates, terms and conditions for interconnection customers 
4

serving electrically proximate or co-located load, and to account for delivered output in assessing 
whether adequate generation is available.
Respectfully submitted,
/s/ Olabanji John Ogunyemi
Olabanji John Ogunyemi
Saint Paul, Minnesota
banjiogunyemi@gmail.com
Filed in his personal capacity
Dated: November 19, 2026
Notes
[1] U.S. Energy Information Administration, Today in Energy, "New U.S. electric generating 
capacity expected to reach a record high in 2026" (Feb. 20, 2026).
[2] Pub. L. No. 119-21 (2025), amending 26 U.S.C. §§ 45Y and 48E for wind and solar 
facilities.
[3] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Queued Up: 2026 Edition, Characteristics of 
Power Plants Seeking Transmission Interconnection (2026).
[4] Show Cause Order (discussing Southwest Power Pool, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,031, at P 64 
(2026)).
[5] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Generator Interconnection Costs to the 
Transmission System in non-ISO Balancing Authorities (finding average estimated costs of 
$671/kW for withdrawn projects against $194/kW for projects that completed all studies). 
The study covers balancing authorities outside the organized markets and is cited for the 
general relationship between cost and withdrawal.
[6] Pub. L. No. 119-21 (2025). The wind and solar termination does not apply to energy storage 
technology, which remains subject to the general phase-down of the section 48E credit.
[7] National Renewable Energy Laboratory, Availability and Performance Loss Factors for U.S. 
PV Fleet Systems, NREL/TP-5K00-88769 (2024) (8.5 GW across 1,128 systems).
